title: easyJet Portugal cabin crew strike: 2–6 October 2026 — your rights
summary: easyJet cabin crew in Portugal strike 2–6 October 2026. Here's whether you're covered for compensation — and why the exact date matters.
body_markdown:
If you're flying easyJet through Lisbon, Porto or Faro between 2 and 6 October, there's a real chance your trip gets caught up in strike action — and if your flight is canceled or delayed by 3 or more hours as a result, you could be owed up to **€600** in[easyJet strike compensation](https://www.airhelp.com/en-int/strike/easyjet-strike-compensation/) . Here's what's happening, and a detail that matters more than usual this time: when you're told about a cancellation could decide whether you're owed anything at all.


## What's happening with the easyJet Portugal strike?


Cabin crew at easyJet's Portuguese bases voted unanimously on 17 September to strike from **2 to 6 October** , with a second walkout planned for **19 to 23 December** . The vote — backed by all 188 staff at an emergency general meeting — was called by SNPVAC, the union representing Portugal's civil aviation flight personnel.


The action covers easyJet's three Portuguese bases:[Lisbon](https://www.airhelp.com/en-int/airports/lisbon-lis/) **,**[Porto](https://www.airhelp.com/en-int/airports/porto-opo/) **and**[Faro](https://www.airhelp.com/en-int/airports/faro-fao/) . SNPVAC estimates around 500 scheduled flights could be grounded during the October strike alone, before accounting for any minimum service levels the authorities may impose.


The union points to frequent last-minute roster changes, an alleged breach of the collective labor agreement, unequal treatment between cabin crew and pilots, and pressure to work overtime due to understaffing. It also says Portuguese crew are paid less than staff at other airlines in Portugal — and less than easyJet pays its own crew elsewhere in its network. easyJet has said it is "extremely disappointed" by the strike call and argues its cabin crew are paid significantly above the Portuguese national average.


The December dates are also on the table, but strike plans can change — we'll update this if anything moves.


## Does a cabin crew strike mean I can claim compensation?


**Yes, in most cases.** Under EC 261, the EU regulation protecting air passengers, an airline can't treat its own staff walking out as "extraordinary circumstances" — the exemption that would otherwise let it avoid paying. easyJet's Portugal cabin crew are easyJet employees, so this dispute sits within the airline's control, not outside it.


That's different from a strike by people who don't work for easyJet — air traffic control staff, for example. A cabin crew walkout is the airline's own staff, so the airline carries the responsibility.


You're likely eligible if:


-


Your flight was canceled, or arrived 3+ hours late at your final destination


-


Your flight departed from an EU airport, or was operated by an EU airline arriving into the EU


-


You weren't told about the disruption far enough in advance — which brings us to the detail that matters most here...


## Why does the 14-day notice window matter so much this time?


This is the part most coverage of this strike is glossing over. EC 261 has one major carve-out even for strikes that are within the airline's control: **if the airline informs you of a cancellation at least 14 days before your original departure, it doesn't have to pay compensation** — you're still entitled to a refund or a rerouted flight, just not the fixed EC 261 payout.


The airline can also avoid paying compensation if it reroutes you on an alternative flight that gets you to your destination only a short time after your original arrival — so if you're quickly rebooked onto another easyJet or partner flight, that's worth keeping in mind too.


SNPVAC's vote was held on **17 September** , only 15 days before the first strike date. That's an unusually tight window for easyJet to notify every affected passenger before the 14-day cutoff — and doing the math on the individual dates shows why:

**All five strike dates are now past their 14-day cutoff.** In plain terms: if easyJet cancels any flight across 2–6 October from this point on, it's doing so after the notice deadline that would have let it avoid paying compensation — which generally means compensation is owed, not just a refund or reroute.


This isn't a guarantee — easyJet may still argue individual passengers were notified in time on a flight-by-flight basis (if it acted very fast right after the 17 September vote), and the rule works differently for delays than for outright cancellations. But for any flight canceled from here on, it's a strong starting position — worth checking properly rather than assuming you're not covered.

## How much compensation could I get?


EC 261 compensation is fixed by flight distance, not ticket price:


Flight distance


Compensation


Up to 1,500 km


Up to €250 per person


1,500–3,500 km


Up to €400 per person


Over 3,500 km


Up to €600 per person


Most easyJet routes touching Lisbon, Porto or Faro fall in the first two bands, though longer easyJet routes could reach the top tier.


## What should I do if I'm flying through Lisbon, Porto or Faro this week?


Even if your specific flight isn't canceled, expect all three airports to be under pressure across 2–6 October as easyJet reshuffles crew and aircraft. A few things help:


-


Check in online and travel with hand luggage where possible


-


Confirm your contact details are correct in your booking, so easyJet can reach you directly if your flight changes


-


Arrive with extra time — at least 2–3 hours before a short-haul departure


-


Keep an eye on the free AirHelp app for real-time flight alerts


## My flight's been canceled — what now?


Start by checking your eligibility — you could be owed up to €600. easyJet is also required to offer you a choice of a full refund, or free rerouting on an alternative flight at the earliest opportunity. If your canceled flight was one leg of a connecting journey, our guide on[what to do if you've missed a flight](https://www.airhelp.com/en-int/blog/i-ve-missed-my-flight-what-are-my-rights-as-a-passenger/) covers how your onward rights work.

## How do I claim?


You can check your eligibility and start a claim in a couple of minutes. If you'd like to understand the process first, our[step-by-step claim walkthrough](https://www.airhelp.com/en-int/blog/how-to-claim-flight-compensation-fast/) covers what happens after you submit — AirHelp deals with easyJet directly and only charges a fee if we win.


If you're a frequent flyer and want ongoing protection against strikes and other disruption, it's also worth knowing what's included with[AirHelp+](https://www.airhelp.com/en-int/airhelp-plus/) — fixed payouts and support that kick in automatically, on top of any EC 261 claim.
